The RCS peak value in the aircraft's head direction decreases non-linearly with increasing wing sweep angle.
The azimuth angle of an RCS peak corresponds exactly to the wing leading edge sweep angle.
At a sweep angle of 33°, the arithmetic average RCS in the head direction is 0.644% of that at 0° sweep angle.
The aircraft model is a single-seat, twin-engine, twin vertical tail design with variable-sweep wings and double S-shaped bend inlets.
Numerical simulations were conducted using PO and ECM methods implemented in MATLAB.
The radar incident wave used in simulations was at X band frequency with horizontal polarization.
A 1:36 scale cast-aluminum model was fabricated and tested in a microwave anechoic chamber to validate the simulation.
The aircraft length is 22 meters.
Sweep angles from 0° to 66° were studied in 3° increments.
The detection probability of the aircraft decreases as the wing sweep angle increases, especially within 100 km detection range.
The RCS arithmetic average values were computed over azimuth intervals of ±10°, ±30°, and ±45°.
At a sweep angle of 54°, the RCS peak value is about 10.3% of the peak value at 0° sweep angle.
The RCS peak values appear symmetrically at positive and negative azimuth angles equal to the sweep angle.
The pitching angle of the incident wave relative to the aircraft affects the RCS and detection probability.
The PO method assumes surface currents equal to those on the tangency plane of the incident point.
ECM calculates edge diffraction using diffraction coefficients and mandatory edge unit vectors.
The study uses a ground-to-air searching radar scenario with the aircraft flying directly towards the radar.
The study provides technical references for conceptual and stealth optimization design of variable-sweep wing aircraft.
The RCS measurement wavelength in the microwave chamber was 0.83 mm.
The probability of detection model incorporates radar parameters such as pulse repetition frequency, antenna gain, noise bandwidth, and system losses.
